clue.text: So part with it and give it to your minister

indicators.note: with it means fashionable and up to date, so the old letters are given a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, the two words read as one string of letters

explanation.surface: A churchgoer is urged to hand money over to the clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part with it' reads as a plea to hand over money, but 'part' belongs to the fodder: the letters of 'So part' rearrange to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastor is a Christian minister in charge of a congregation, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: see Lena has met an extra-terrestrial!

indicators.note: a loose signal: an encounter shakes things up, so the letters of the name come out in another order

parts.note: the name taken as written, plus an I that no word of the printed clue supplies

explanation.surface: Look: Lena has had a close encounter with a being from space.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as printed is short of an I: Lena rearranged with I gives the answer, but nothing in the clue supplies the I, which may have been lost from the start of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An alien is a being from another world, which is what an extra-terrestrial is.

clue.text: He met one playing a tune!

indicators.note: playing suggests fooling about with the letters, so they are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: A man encountered a busker performing a melody.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the main melody of a piece of music, or a signature tune.

clue.text: opposed Ed going out with my sister

indicators.note: going out reads as dating, but it also means leaving the usual place, so the letters are moved about

explanation.surface: Someone objected to Ed dating their sister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going out with' reads as dating, but 'going out' is the signal to rearrange the letters of Ed and sister.
explanation.definitionFit: To resist something is to fight against it, so resisted and opposed are past-tense synonyms.

clue.text: Dad went back and Ed copied him

definitions.note: the verb copied, with its object

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the word for father is read from right to left

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: Ed imitated his father as Dad walked away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dad' looks like the person copied, but it only supplies the informal word for father, turned around.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape someone is to mimic them, often clumsily, so aped means copied.

clue.text: Has a shop visited by a king, a queen and a Commanding Officer

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the person who does it

parts.note: GR is Georgius Rex, King George
OC is the military abbreviation for Officer Commanding
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper boasts of royal and military customers.
explanation.walkthrough: GR (King George's cipher) and ER (Elizabeth Regina) are royal monograms; OC, Officer Commanding, stands for the commanding officer. The pieces are taken in a different order from the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A grocer is a trader who keeps a shop selling food and household goods, the one who has a shop.

clue.text: Mum takes Sue to a place of interest

indicators.note: takes means holds within, so the mother word is wrapped around the name
a loose signal: the name is changed to something else as it goes in

explanation.surface: A mother brings her daughter Sue on an outing to a tourist sight.
explanation.walkthrough: SUE goes between the U and the final M of MUM, with its letters rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A museum is a building of exhibits that visitors go to see, a typical place of interest.

clue.text: I'm up to more dealings in this shop!

indicators.note: dealings suggests the letters are dealt out like cards, so they come back in a different order

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper boasts of doing a roaring trade in his store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm up to more dealings' reads as a trader's boast; the letters of 'I'm up' and 'more' are the fodder, with 'to' only joining them.
explanation.definitionFit: An emporium is a large store selling many kinds of goods, a grand word for a shop.

clue.text: Several of them working underwater?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old word for various or sundry
second meaning: people who work beneath the surface of the water

explanation.surface: A question about how many of a crew are busy beneath the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: The archaic adjective 'divers' (as in 'divers persons') means several; the same letters are the plural of diver.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaic English used the adjective for various or sundry things, and the plural noun names people who swim beneath the water.

clue.text: Practically indicated that he was to be formally charged

indicators.note: practically means almost all of it, so one letter of the word that follows is dropped

explanation.surface: Someone all but signalled that a suspect would face charges.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the A from INDICATED to leave INDICTED, a word that sounds almost the same; the setter removes an inner letter rather than the usual last one.
explanation.definitionFit: To indict someone is to accuse them formally of a serious crime, which is being formally charged.

clue.text: Implies that it's considered finer to point in the end

definitions.note: loose: strictly the speaker implies and the listener infers

indicators.note: something considered is turned over in the mind, so the word after it is turned about into a new order

parts.note: a point of the compass: S for south

explanation.surface: Someone hints that a sharpened point at the tip is thought better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the end' places the compass point last. Using 'infers' for 'implies' is a common loose usage that purists object to.
explanation.definitionFit: In everyday loose usage to infer is treated as to suggest or hint, the sense of imply.

clue.text: A fool? Lost nothing on that horse!

indicators.note: lost means gone missing, so the fool word is without the thing named next

parts.note: nothing is zero, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A punter who backed a losing horse is mocked as a fool, though he broke even.
explanation.walkthrough: FOOL loses an O, and the A goes into the gap: the A takes the place of the lost nothing. There is no separate word signalling the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: A foal is a young horse, so the general word stands for it by example.

clue.text: How to taunt the missus by fits of ill-temper

indicators.note: how to asks for a method of making something, so the following letters are worked into a new arrangement

parts.note: the missus is a wife, abbreviated Mrs

explanation.surface: Advice on goading one's wife by throwing tantrums.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The missus' is slang for a wife, giving the title MRS; with TAUNT it makes eight letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Tantrums are childish outbursts of anger, which is what fits of ill-temper describes.

clue.text: Listen! In New Guinea, they're settling down comfortably

indicators.note: a loose signal: the clue says the letters are already in the new form named after, so they must be rearranged

parts.note: NG is the abbreviation for New Guinea

explanation.surface: A call to hear how people in New Guinea are making themselves at home.
explanation.walkthrough: The signal is weak; the letters of LISTEN and NG are simply rearranged. NG is the standard abbreviation for New Guinea.
explanation.definitionFit: To nestle is to settle snugly into a comfortable position, so the present participle matches the phrase.

clue.text: Of course, Paul! Natives wear this bone

indicators.note: to wear something is to carry it on you, so the answer is carried within the words before

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Someone assures Paul that tribespeople do wear a bone as an ornament.
explanation.definitionFit: The ulna is one of the two long bones of the forearm, a specific example of a bone.

clue.text: Crashes and Les and I just get a cold!

indicators.note: a loose signal: the named pieces simply become something new when they come together

explanation.surface: Two people complain that after their car crashes they just catch a chill.
explanation.walkthrough: The signal is weak; the letters of Les, I and cold are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Collides means comes into violent contact with something, which is what a vehicle does when it crashes.

clue.text: No bore may become king in Fairyland

indicators.note: may become says the letters can turn into something else, so they are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone who is no bore might be crowned king of the fairies.
explanation.definitionFit: Oberon is the king of the fairies in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream and in medieval legend.

clue.text: Where a fat queen keeps all the food

definitions.text: Where a fat queen keeps all the food

parts.note: lard is pig fat used in cooking
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A greedy queen hoards every scrap of food in her pantry.
explanation.walkthrough: ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen. The whole clue describes a pantry, while its middle words build the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A larder is a cool room or cupboard for storing food, so the whole clue describes one.

clue.text: Dear! It disturbs one — that sort of talk!

indicators.note: to disturb is to stir up and put out of place, so the words before are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Someone recoils from an upsetting style of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A tirade is a long angry speech of criticism, the kind of talk the clue objects to.

clue.text: I'd take the rap but you're so quick!

explanation.surface: Someone offers to accept blame for a speedy friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The two pieces appear in the clue in the opposite order: 'I'd' first, but it comes second in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapid means fast or swift, a direct synonym of quick.

clue.text: I'd stay with Reg, but what a misery!

definitions.note: loose: a dirge is a mournful song, an expression of misery

indicators.note: a loose signal: the words are kept together and mixed into one new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone would stay with Reg, but finds him gloomy company.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirge is a slow lament for the dead, a gloomy song that stands loosely for misery itself.

clue.text: As an act of retaliation, I am left with all the repairs

indicators.note: a loose signal: the speaker says they are left with the repair job, so the pieces are fixed into a new order

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone complains that they've been landed with all the mending as punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: The signal is weak; L and the letters of 'repairs' rearrange to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprisal is an act of retaliation against an enemy, so the two phrases are synonyms.

clue.text: Little Sally and I are on our yacht

indicators.note: a loose signal: the two are placed together, one tucked inside the shortened name

parts.note: Sal is a short form of the name Sally

explanation.surface: A couple boast of being out on their boat together.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes inside SAL. The definition is a verb with a plural subject: Sally and I sail.
explanation.definitionFit: To sail is to travel on a boat with sails, which is what people on a yacht do.

clue.text: I'll tell you a secret! I'm to separate!

definitions.note: the verb is acted out by the speaker rather than defined

explanation.surface: A confiding friend who also announces a break-up.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an example: the speaker is about to impart something.
explanation.definitionFit: To impart is to pass on or disclose information, which is what telling a secret does.

clue.text: Put a coin in your shoe — it will make it stick together

definitions.text: it will make it stick together
definitions.note: noun defined by what it does

indicators.note: to put things somewhere is to place them, so the letters are placed again in another order

explanation.surface: Folk advice: slip a coin into your shoe to keep things together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put … in' looks like an insertion, but the eight letters of coin and shoe are rearranged instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Cohesion is the force or quality that makes the parts of something bond and hold together.

clue.text: Gad! Obtain one for me! Could be useful!

definitions.note: loose: describes a gadget rather than naming it

parts.note: taken as written: an old mild oath

explanation.surface: An excited shopper asks someone to fetch them a handy device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gad!' is an old-fashioned exclamation, a softened form of God.
explanation.definitionFit: A gadget is a small handy device, something whose whole point is that it could be useful.
